title: Travelling salesman

problem.name: Travelling salesman problem
problem.statement_latex:
Given a weighted graph $G=(V,E,w)$, $|V|=n$, find a Hamiltonian cycle $C$ minimizing $\sum_{e\in C}w(e)$, or report infeasibility. Integer weights have maximum magnitude $L$ and are binary encoded. The problem models routing and cyclic sequencing.
The general quantum bound uses QRAM time and the bounded-degree bounds use quantum gate time, while classical bounds use RAM time with polynomial weight-bit costs.
problem.statement_text: Given a weighted graph $G=(V,E,w)$, $|V|=n$, find a Hamiltonian cycle $C$ minimizing $\sum_{e\in C}w(e)$, or report infeasibility. quantum.headline_latex: $O^*(1.728^n)$, quantum subset dynamic programming; $O^*(1.110^n)$ and $O^*(1.301^n)$ on degree-three and degree-four graphs, quantum backtracking.
quantum.headline_text: $O^*(1.728^n)$, quantum subset dynamic programming; $O^*(1.110^n)$ and $O^*(1.301^n)$ on degree-three and degree-four graphs, quantum backtracking.
quantum.details_latex: The general algorithm assumes coherent access to its exponentially large precomputed table. The bounded-degree algorithms use polynomial workspace and have additional factors $\log L\log\log L$ for integer weights. Their graph restrictions are part of the stated comparisons.
quantum.details_text: The general algorithm assumes coherent access to its exponentially large precomputed table. The bounded-degree algorithms use polynomial workspace and have additional factors $\log L\log\log L$ for integer weights. Their graph restrictions are part of the stated comparisons.

classical.headline_latex: $O(n^2 2^n)$, Held--Karp dynamic programming; $O^*(1.1757^n)$ and $O^*(1.4214^n)$ on degree-three and degree-four graphs, sparse-graph path-decomposition algorithms.
classical.headline_text: $O(n^2 2^n)$, Held–Karp dynamic programming; $O^*(1.1757^n)$ and $O^*(1.4214^n)$ on degree-three and degree-four graphs, sparse-graph path-decomposition algorithms.
classical.details_latex: Held--Karp uses $O(n2^n)$ words and optimizes paths indexed by a visited set and endpoint. The sparse-graph bounds use exponential memory and the weighted connectivity algorithm of Gaspers. A polynomial-space cubic-graph comparator runs in $O^*(1.232^n)$ time. Thus each quantum bound is compared with the applicable degree and memory regime, with the bit cost of objective arithmetic retained in polynomial factors.

strength.description_latex: Polynomial speedups through smaller exponential constants. General subset dynamic programming uses minimum finding and amplitude amplification; the bounded-degree constructions use quantum backtracking.
strength.description_text: Polynomial speedups through smaller exponential constants. General subset dynamic programming uses minimum finding and amplitude amplification; the bounded-degree constructions use quantum backtracking.

evidence.description_latex: Rigorous upper bounds and partial evidence relative to the strongest displayed classical algorithms in their respective graph classes.

hardware.description_latex: The general algorithm needs polynomial active registers and exponential QRAM. The bounded-degree versions need polynomial logical workspace but exponentially long coherent tree searches. Both useful regimes require fault tolerance; degree restrictions reduce the exponential time base.
